title: Algorithmic Management and Employee Well-Being: A Text Mining and Behavioral Science Review (2020–2026)
content: Algorithmic management (AM)—the use of algorithms and data-driven systems to allocate, monitor, evaluate and discipline work—has expanded from platform labor into conventional organizations and is increasingly linked to employee well-being. This review maps 255 publications from the reference corpus supplied for this study (nominal window 2020–2026) by combining a transparent title-level text-mining workflow, a behavioral-science coding frame and a reference-by-reference narrative synthesis in which every record is discussed. Methods: titles were parsed, tokenized and screened with stop-word removal; term and bigram frequencies, six theme codes and theme co-occurrence were computed, and the records were then synthesized in seventeen thematic sections covering conceptual foundations, platform-worker evidence, double-edged effects, autonomy, technostress, surveillance, fairness, trust, behavioral outcomes, AI adoption, AI-based well-being tools, careers, Industry 5.0 and sectoral contexts. Results: output is strongly recent (175 of 255 records, 69%, fall in 2025–2026), and the literature concentrates on well-being, burnout and stress (152 titles), AI-enabled HRM and analytics (107) and gig/platform work (68), whereas fairness, transparency and ethics are comparatively less studied (22). The synthesis shows that effects are conditional: algorithmic control can exhaust or energize depending on appraisal, autonomy, fairness, support and the specific control dimension, and that dignity-related pathways complement stress pathways. Conclusions: AM research is dominated by outcome-focused studies of stress and well-being, with ethical and design-oriented work lagging behind; future studies should test moderators such as autonomy and explainability with full-text corpora, longitudinal designs and harmonized measurement.
